The Mountain plover (Charadrius montanus) is a moderately sized shorebird breeding on short-grass prairies of the North American Great Plains. Eggs are deposited in a simple scrape, with females producing a range of 1 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 4 eggs per clutch]. Field observations indicate this species is capable of two distinct nesting attempts each year [F_R_i = two distinct nesting attempts each year], a strategy that may compensate for high nest predation rates. The initial wet weight of newly captured adults in breeding condition has been recorded at approximately 13 grams [Ww0 = approximately 13 grams], though early-season individuals may weigh slightly less. Under the thermal conditions typical of the chick-rearing period, which occur at an ambient temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental events unfolds; fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at approximately 40 days after hatching [tx = approximately 40 days after hatching], a period that aligns with the growth trajectory of semi-precocial young.

Nestling development begins with clutches incubated for a duration that is heavily influenced by substrate temperature. When eggs are maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], pipping and hatching occur at about 29 days [ab = about 29 days], a figure that falls within the 28- to 31-day range reported across the species' breeding range. The wet weight of a newly hatched chick, measured within hours of emergence, averages 9 grams [Wwb = 9 grams]; this birth mass is modest relative to the adult size and reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the altricial-precocial continuum typical of charadriiforms. The energetic demands of the nestling period are considerable, and the rate of mass gain during the first week is a strong predictor of subsequent survival. The heat of the prairie environment accelerates metabolic processes, influencing the speed of feather development and the timing of first flight. Additional studies have shown that the pre-fledging period, which involves rapid wing feather elongation, demands a consistent supply of high-protein insect prey, and nestlings that fall below a threshold mass gain often experience delayed fledging or reduced post-fledging survival.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a larger ultimate wet weight than males. The maximum recorded wet weight for a breeding adult female is 114 grams [Wwi = 114 grams], a value that represents the upper asymptote of the growth curve for this sex. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight of male Mountain plovers typically reaches 102 grams [Wwi = 102 grams], a difference of roughly 12 percent that is consistent with the reversed sexual size dimorphism observed in many shorebirds where females are larger. This size disparity likely relates to the energetic demands of egg production, as a larger female body can store greater reserves for clutch formation. The observed range of adult masses also varies seasonally, with birds at their heaviest just prior to migration.

The attainment of sexual maturity in the Mountain plover occurs later than in many small-bodied passerines, reflecting a slower life-history pace. Puberty, defined as the first period of gonadal activity capable of supporting reproduction, is reached at approximately 120 days after hatching [tp = approximately 120 days after hatching] when birds are exposed to typical summer thermal conditions (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]). However, first breeding is typically deferred until the subsequent calendar year, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at a full 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This delay between physiological maturity and actual reproductive effort is a common pattern among migratory species, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition and acquire a breeding territory on the prairie landscape before committing to the high costs of egg production and parental care.

Longevity data for the Mountain plover, derived from mark-recapture studies and banding returns, indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when individuals are active during the warm months at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This is a relatively long lifespan for a Charadrius species of this body size, and it suggests a life-history strategy that favors adult survival over high annual fecundity. The documented ability to produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], combined with an extended reproductive lifespan, allows a single adult female to contribute significantly to population recruitment over her lifetime. The ecological constraints of the short-grass prairie, including unpredictable precipitation and fluctuating food availability, likely select for bet-hedging reproductive tactics that moderate annual output in favor of consistent, multi-year breeding attempts.
